headline: RBA 25bp hike to 4.6% expected; low tolerance for inflation is the key driver, not committing to further hikes
reasoning: Fenner expected a 25bp hike, citing the RBA's and Governor Bullock's clearly signalled low tolerance for inflation as the primary driver. She noted some softening in the labour market but did not see it as sufficient justification to hold. She flagged that the statement referenced upside inflation risks materialising (as flagged in August), energy price pressures from the Middle East feeding into inflation, and AI-related demand driving tech goods prices globally. She noted Q2 GDP came in stronger than anticipated. A larger move than 25bp was not expected as it would signal inflation is getting out of control.
quote: I don't think there is. Well, there is some economics. I mean, if you sat there and said, OK, the labour market is showing some signs of softening. But I mean, the the senior officials, Governor Bullock, they've all clearly shown, you know, shown a low tolerance for inflation. And that's going to be the key reason for for why they're going to raise rates. So 25 basis, 25 expecting no more.
episode_title: Rates Live | RBA pulls the trigger

headline: Wants clarity from Bullock on whether this is the last hike and on the RBA's read of the labour market given the dual mandate
reasoning: Sian Fenner indicated she wanted to hear from Michelle Bullock whether this rate hike is the last, and what the RBA believes it will achieve for the economy. She also sought greater clarity on the RBA's view of the labour market, noting the wide divergence between Treasury and RBA estimates of the non-inflationary unemployment rate. She stressed that while the RBA is currently focused almost entirely on inflation, the dual mandate means employment should not be ignored.
quote: I do want to get some idea about just where she thinks at this last rate hike. What is that she going to do for the economy or maybe wishful thinking on that front. I also would like to get a better read on that you at the labour market about, you know, there is a wide range, as was mentioned, you know, the Treasury is, you know, got a much higher at sort of lower unemployment rate for that. It's non inflationary versus the RBA. But so you know, what is their take on on the labour market because it's ultimately is a dual mandate. I mean, at the moment, the weight is very much on inflation, low tolerance for for the persistence that we've had in high inflation that lately.

headline: Housing market weakness adding further drag on consumer spending via subdued wealth effect and lower furnishing impulse
reasoning: Fenner highlights that the housing market decline is affecting consumer spending not just through sentiment and the wealth effect from falling prices, but also through reduced spending on related goods such as furniture for new homes. This secondary channel adds an extra weight on household consumption that is unlikely to reverse soon.
quote: The housing market isn't just, you know, prices. It's how, you know, if you buy a new house that you'll be, you know, possibly going off to buy some more furnishings, you know, you know, new couch for your new house. And, you know, that's, that's just an extra weight on the household consumes that we're not going to see that impulse coming through.

headline: November RBA hike is on the table; unanimous decision signals data-dependent bias with upside risk from sticky inflation around 3% and elevated oil/freight costs
reasoning: Sian Fenner expected a split decision but the unanimous vote signals a firmer consensus. She sees the next move as highly data-dependent, hinging on CPI and labour market outcomes. She forecasts trimmed mean CPI at 3.6% and headline rising to 4%, with a real risk of inflation staying sticky around or just above 3%. Oil prices and rising freight levies from the Middle East conflict are upside risks. She notes the RBA is already in restrictive territory but cannot easily address supply-driven inflation without hitting consumers harder.
quote: It's putting the risk to a November hike. It's very much on the table. What are your expectations for that CPI print tomorrow? We're looking for it to be 3.6 for the trim main, the headline going up to 4%. So you know, we're at another sort of 3.6 and even for the Q2Q3 you're at 3.5. It's 3.3 at the end of the year. So it's, I think the concern is that even if you get some disinflation, is it enough to get it, you know, quickly down below that 3% And there's a real risk of it sort of being sticky around sort of that 3% or just above.

headline: Aussie consumers pulling back on discretionary spend as fuel prices and high interest rates squeeze household budgets
reasoning: Fenner notes that while households showed some resilience partly aided by the fuel excise tax, rising fuel prices and higher interest rates are now squeezing budgets. Card tracker data for September signals a shift away from discretionary spending such as dining out and clothing as households face higher fuel bills and debt servicing costs. Consumer confidence has also fallen back to its lowest level since May, reinforcing the picture of a struggling consumer.
quote: We had been sort of seeing some kind of resilience with households. And I think part of that was actually the fuel excise tax. So you know that that did help matters. But of course, with fuel prices increasing again, it is putting the squeeze on households, adding to the fact that we've got higher interest rates as well. And so we're getting some signs both from what you're seeing in the monthly household spending indicator, but some of our car tracker about how this has flown on in September is that there's some signs that actually it's mean that you're getting some movement away from the discretionary spend.

headline: Post-hike statement cites stronger Q2 GDP, Middle East energy price pass-through, and AI-driven tech goods inflation as upside risks materialising
reasoning: Fenner's immediate read of the statement highlighted that Q2 GDP came in stronger than the RBA anticipated even as it slowed. The RBA cited inflation remaining elevated with upside risks from August materialising, specifically pointing to Middle East energy prices feeding into broader inflation and AI-related demand driving rapid growth in global tech goods prices. These were the key justifications for the move.

So that's one front of that. And of course then there's that sort of inflation are at the inflation risk to this as well. Yeah. So the explanation is inflation remains elevated and some of the upside risk flagged in August are materialising. So clearly they are concerned. They obviously cite the what's going on in the Middle East and where those energy prices and how that's feeding into inflation at the moment. headline: Australian consumer sentiment improving but remains at historically low levels, with inflation expectations still elevated
reasoning: Consumer sentiment is still pessimistic overall and near 50-year lows, but there has been improvement since bottoming out following the Middle East conflict. Consumers are becoming more optimistic about family finances and the broader economy, suggesting a levels-versus-trend dynamic. Inflation expectations remain strong, partly influenced by the rolling out of fuel excise tax discounts.
quote: So with consumers of course, we're seeing that they're quite pessimistic in terms of overall sentiment. But we are seeing an improvement in several areas. So we are seeing consumers becoming more optimistic in terms of how they're feeling about their family finances as well as around the economy. Um, I think this is a levels versus trend story. So we are seeing improvements since bottoming out following the Middle East conflict. But it does look like sentiment is overall improving while still remaining pessimistic of course. Still on very low levels.
episode_title: Inflation may look cooler, but Westpac sees heat underneath

headline: Westpac sees trimmed mean inflation at 3.5% for July, still above RBA target, with core pressures remaining sticky
reasoning: Sharma expects trimmed mean CPI of 0.4% in July, a pick-up from June's 0.3%, with the year-ended core rate at 3.5% — still above the RBA's 2-3% target band. Broad-based price pressures persist across multiple categories. While June quarter CPI came in softer than expected, it remains strong overall and not consistent with the RBA's target. The disinflationary impulse is expected to come as the economy slows and labour market slack increases.
quote: For trimmed mean, we're expecting a 0.4%. That's a bit of a pick up from June where we got 0.3%, but we are expecting a slight dip in year ended. And so therefore, what would be the annual core rate that you're looking for? So we're looking for a 3.5%. So that's still above what the RBA wants.
episode_title: Inflation may look cooler, but Westpac sees heat underneath

headline: New dwelling cost inflation running at 5.7% year-ended and expected to remain persistent, driven by materials costs and competition from data centre construction
reasoning: New housing inflation is one of the key pressure points in the CPI basket and has significant weight, suggesting persistence in trimmed mean inflation. Materials prices have been rising due to Middle East conflict. There is also competition for resources between nonresidential building (particularly data centre build-out) and residential building. Westpac expects a 0.4% rise in new dwelling costs for July, taking the year-ended rate to 5.7%, with disinflation from there expected to be slow.
quote: New housing inflation is, of course, one of the key pressure points in the CPI basket currently. It doesn't bode well for trimmed mean inflation because it does suggest there will be some persistence there just given its weight in the CPI basket. So the key things that are affecting it there is what's happening in the Middle East that's seeing materials price increase by quite a lot. We're also seeing some competition for resources between nonresidential building and residential building, particularly as data center build out phase expands. So we expect a 0.4% rise in new dwelling costs for July. That will take the year ended rate to 5.7. And the disinflation from there is quite slow to progress.
episode_title: Inflation may look cooler, but Westpac sees heat underneath

headline: Forecasts July CPI headline at 3.3% year-ended, well below June's 3.8%, driven largely by base effects in electricity prices
reasoning: Neha Sharma expects a 0.8% monthly lift in July CPI but a significant drop in the year-ended rate to 3.3% from 3.8% in June. The main driver of the decline is base effects from strong electricity price rises last year not repeating. Upward pressures include auto fuel (excise discount rolling from 32c to 16c), seasonal holiday travel increases, and water and property rates. Electricity, via lower default market offers in most states, is expected to be the main offset.
quote: So in terms of the July CPI data that's coming out tomorrow, we're expecting a 0.8% lift in the month. That's quite a strong number at face value. But the year ended pace, we are actually expecting quite a significant drop to 3.3% from 3.8% in June. And a lot of this is due to base effects. So we saw electricity prices last year come up quite strongly, and we're not expecting the same level of impulse there.
episode_title: Inflation may look cooler, but Westpac sees heat underneath

headline: Westpac base case is no further RBA rate hikes, with cuts expected from August 2027, but upside inflation risks remain
reasoning: Westpac's base case is for no further rate hikes, with rate cuts expected from August 27 onwards. However, there is a risk of further hikes if upside inflation risks materialise, as the RBA has flagged openness to hiking if necessary. Sharma expects the unemployment rate to move towards 5% as economic slack builds, which should help bring inflation back towards the RBA target band. The disinflationary impulse is seen as coming primarily from a slowing economy and a looser labour market.
quote: Well our base case is now for no further rate hikes. Um, and until August 27th where we're expecting cuts from then onwards. But there is of course a risk for further hikes. The RBA has said that they're open to further hikes if upside risks to inflation materialise. We don't necessarily see that happening. Of course June quarter CPI came in a bit softer than expected. It's still strong overall and like you said, not consistent with the RBA's target band for July.
episode_title: Inflation may look cooler, but Westpac sees heat underneath
